title: Digital Art
objective: After this level you can explain how computers and screens have changed the way art is made.
summary: Computer art began with plotter drawings in 1965. Nees's Schotter turned randomness into art, Cohen's AARON drew by itself, and in 2021 an NFT sold for $69.3 million.

cards.headline: In February 1965, a gallery in Stuttgart showed drawings made by a computer.
cards.body: Georg Nees, a mathematician working as a software engineer at Siemens, wrote programs, and a drawing machine turned them into ink on paper. It was one of the first shows of computer graphics anywhere. For the first time, an artist's main tool was a set of instructions.

cards.headline: Order, then chaos
cards.body: Picture Nees's Schotter ("gravel"), printed between 1968 and 1970. At the top, neat rows of squares sit perfectly straight. Row by row they tilt and slip a little more, until the bottom looks like a spilled box of tiles. Nees built random variables into his program, so the orderly squares descend into chaos. He was exploring order and disorder in a picture.

cards.headline: A program that draws by itself
cards.body: In 1973 the painter Harold Cohen started AARON, a program that made drawings on its own, following rules he wrote. Early on, a small robot "turtle" holding a marker crawled over the paper to draw them. For about 20 years Cohen colored the drawings by hand; AARON only learned to color them itself in 1995. So who's the artist: Cohen, AARON, or both?

cards.fact: In 2021, a digital file sold for $69.3 million.
cards.context: Mike Winkelmann, known as Beeple, made an image every day from 2007, then combined 5,000 of them into one collage. In March 2021 Christie's sold it as an NFT, a token on a blockchain that certifies ownership of a digital item, for $69.3 million: the first purely digital artwork sold that way by a major auction house. Remember Level 2's question: what counts as art? Screens reopened it.

questions.prompt: How did Georg Nees make the squares in Schotter drift into chaos?

options.label: He built random variables into his program
He shook the paper while the machine drew
options.rationale: The disorder came from the program.

options.label: He drew the lower rows by hand
options.rationale: A drawing machine made it from his program.

options.label: He photographed spilled tiles
options.rationale: That's just the picture it resembles.

questions.explanation: Nees introduced random variables into the program, so the orderly squares descend into chaos.

questions.prompt: What made Harold Cohen's AARON different from a drawing tool?

options.label: It made drawings on its own, following Cohen's rules
It copied Cohen's paintings exactly
options.rationale: It made new drawings from rules.

options.label: It was a paintbrush with a motor
It could color from the very start
options.rationale: It only learned to color in 1995.

questions.explanation: AARON made drawings by itself, following rules Cohen wrote; a robot turtle first put them on paper.

questions.prompt: In 1926, customs said Bird in Space was just metal. What did the $69.3 million for Beeple's Everydays buy?

options.label: The only copy of the image
A token certifying ownership of the file
A bronze sculpture of the collage

questions.explanation: It was sold as an NFT: a blockchain token that certifies ownership of a digital item.
